title: Trump minaccia l'iran mentre promette calo dei prezzi energetici

occhiello: TRUMP MINACCIA L'IRAN MENTRE PROMETTE CALO DEI PREZZI ENERGETICI
lead: Washington, 30 settembre 2026. Il Presidente degli Stati Uniti, Donald Trump, ha dichiarato di essere pronto a far saltare in aria gli iraniani a causa dello stallo nei negoziati internazionali. Durante un colloquio con i giornalisti, il capo della Casa Bianca ha definito le autorità di Teheran come pazzi, sostenendo che una decisione definitiva sull'uso della forza contro il Paese mediorientale sia ormai prossima. Il Presidente ha inoltre legato l'esito del conflitto al costo del carburante per i cittadini americani.
corpo1: Le parole di Donald Trump sono arrivate in risposta a una precisa sollecitazione della stampa riguardo alle strategie negoziali dell'amministrazione americana. Il Presidente ha replicato con una sequenza verbale ripetuta per sottolineare la gravità dell'opzione militare sul tavolo, affermando che Forse li facciamo saltare in aria. Forse li facciamo saltare in aria. Dobbiamo prendere questa decisione. Li facciamo saltare in aria. Il momento sta arrivando. Secondo quanto riportato dall'Agenzia Giornalistica Italia, il leader statunitense ha insistito sul fatto che il momento per prendere questa decisione stia arrivando, definendo gli interlocutori iraniani come pazzi. La retorica presidenziale non si è limitata alla minaccia bellica, ma ha toccato anche le implicazioni economiche dirette per gli Stati Uniti. Trump ha infatti previsto che, non appena la guerra giungerà al termine, un evento che il Presidente ha definito imminente, i prezzi del carburante subiranno un rapido calo. Questa dichiarazione, rilasciata il 30 settembre 2026, segna un inasprimento drastico dei toni rispetto alla fase di stallo diplomatico che ha caratterizzato le relazioni tra Washington e Teheran nelle ultime settimane. Il Presidente ha lasciato intendere che la pazienza della Casa Bianca è esaurita, ponendo l'azione militare come una scelta concreta e non più come una mera ipotesi di scuola.

Anna Colombo (journalist for La Lente Mattutina). Geopolitical, cynical, realistic, sharp, no moralizing, no "good vs evil", no rhetorical questions. Focuses on the link between global politics and everyday life (prices, energy).
Replace the existing "Corpo 2" of an article about Trump's threats to Iran and promises of lower energy prices.
Trump's threats/promises (Sept 30, 2026).

           Source 1/2:* Trump spoke at the 81st UN General Assembly in NY. He claims military action is necessary to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. He claims he has achieved an "Iran without a nuclear weapon." He promises gas prices will crash after the war. He mentions a new oil exploration agreement with Venezuela (following the replacement of Maduro with Delcy Rodriguez). He claims US + Venezuela control 60% of global oil.
           Source 3:* Iran warned it will hit US infrastructure (energy facilities in the Gulf) if Trump acts. US Marines and heavy landing craft are moving toward the region.
           Contextual Note:* Trump is using the UN platform to justify the military stance and uses the "oil price drop" as a domestic political selling point.
           Scenario Selection:* Scenario 4 (Commercial/Energy) and Scenario 1 (War/Conflict) are most relevant. I need to connect the military movement to the energy market and the geopolitical shifts (Venezuela).

       Opening:* Move from the rhetoric of the Oval Office/UN to the actual geopolitical chess pieces. The "why" behind the threat.
       The Military/Conflict aspect:* Mention the Marines/landing craft moving to the Gulf. Mention Iran's counter-threat (hitting energy infrastructure). This isn't just talk; it's positioning.
       The Energy/Economic aspect (The "Why"):* Connect the war to the oil market. Trump's math: War -> Control -> Lower prices. Mention the Venezuela factor (the new deal with Rodriguez/post-Maduro Venezuela) and the claim of controlling 60% of global oil.
       The "Realism" (The "Translation"):* When Trump says "prices will drop," he's implying a total restructuring of the energy supply chain under US hegemony.
       Closing:* A projection/consequence. If the US/Venezuela axis holds and the Gulf is neutralized, the impact is a shift in energy dominance, but the immediate risk is a massive spike in prices due to the very conflict he's using to promise lower prices.

       Drafting - Step 1 (Military/Tactical):* The rhetoric at the UN General Assembly is backed by physical movement. While Trump speaks of "winning quickly," the US Marines and heavy landing craft are already deploying toward the Gulf. This isn't a bluff; it's a logistical buildup. Iran, in response, has already signaled its intent to strike back, specifically targeting US energy infrastructure in the Persian Gulf. The risk is a classic feedback loop: a military operation intended to secure energy supplies could instead trigger a massive disruption of the very pipelines and tankers it aims to protect.

       Drafting - Step 2 (Geopolitical/Energy):* The underlying logic of the Trump administration is a radical consolidation of energy control. The president's claim of a "post-war price crash" relies on a new geopolitical architecture: the axis between Washington and a post-Maduro Venezuela. By securing an oil exploration agreement with the Delcy Rodriguez administration, Trump is attempting to create a duopoly—alongside the United States—that would control roughly 60% of the global oil supply. The goal is clear: bypass the traditional volatility of the Middle East by leveraging South American reserves, effectively turning the energy market into a tool of American strategic dominance.

       Drafting - Step 3 (The "Translation" and Closing):* When the White House speaks of "stability," it means the ability to dictate terms through sheer volume of production and military presence. If the deployment in the Gulf succeeds in neutralizing Tehran's nuclear ambitions without a protracted insurgency, the sudden influx of controlled supply could indeed depress prices. However, if Iran follows through on its threats against Gulf infrastructure, the immediate reality for the markets—and for European consumers sensitive to supply shocks—will be a period of extreme volatility and price spikes that no amount of Venezuelan oil can offset in the short term.
